inline.s: Here the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing reveals the methods of holding the sutra, holding the mantra, and reciting the Buddha's name:
Directly illuminate the mind-ground; dissolve everything back into self-nature, and cultivate as taught.

[As for holding the sutra and mantra] Holding the sutra and mantra is to hold one's own mind, causing it to correspond to the sutra and mantra. So the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing thereupon revealed:
“The essential
is
(the key is)
to directly illuminate the mind-ground,”
“every phrase should dissolve back into self-nature,”
“therefore, knowing this, when you hold this sutra, you should immediately cultivate in accordance with this sutra
(cultivating as it teaches)

. [Mind-ground] The mind is the root of all dharmas and can give rise to all dharmas, so the mind is called the 'mind-ground.' Also, because practitioners act in accordance with the mind, the mind is called the 'mind-ground.' [Directly illuminate the mind-ground] Directly strip away the deluded thoughts and greed, hatred, and delusion within the mind, causing the mind to return to clarity. [Every phrase dissolves back into self-nature] Every phrase is carried out upon one's own mind and conduct, causing self-nature to turn from delusion to awareness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is sentient beings; when self-nature is aware, that is the Buddha.”
(See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha
article.)

blocks.text: Entering the Mountain to Await Death

inline.s: [The old monk Tianran, because of a long illness that would not heal, wished to enter Jingshan to await death, so as to leave his bones in the Putong stupa. The Bodhisattva said: 'You wish to live in the mountain awaiting death — this is courting trouble where there is none! Are you worrying that your few old bones have nowhere to be put? You do not know that once the eyes' light falls to the ground
(a person's death)
, and the two legs stretch straight out, then let them hack and chop you with knife and axe
zhuó,
to cut and hack with a knife or an axe)
, burn you with fire and soak you in water — all of it is unrelated to you
(all of it is unrelated to you)
, yet you still make long-term plans for it — this is too foolish. Moreover, this body while alive is already of no benefit; how much the more after death!']

The old monk Tianran, because of a long illness that would not heal, planned to enter Jingshan to await death, so as to place his remains in the Putong stupa. The Bodhisattva said: 'You wish to live in the mountain awaiting death — this is looking for trouble where there is none! Are you still worrying that your few old bones have nowhere to settle? You do not know that once the eyes close and the two feet stretch straight out, and the consciousness (self-nature) has departed, then let them hack and chop you with knife and axe, burn you with fire and soak you in water — it is all unrelated to you; yet you still make long-term plans for it, and this is too foolish. Moreover, this body while alive is already of no benefit — how much the more after death?'

[You should now simplify and set aside all the various matters, and single-mindedly hold the single phrase 'Amitabha Buddha,' never casting it aside for a single thought-moment; then Amitabha Buddha will be your good companion. When the great limit
(the time of death)
arrives, he will appear in person to guide you, and you will be reborn in Ultimate Bliss — how is this not superior
(how is this not better)
to entering the mountain to await death? Moreover,
(and furthermore)

birth, aging, sickness, and death are the unavoidable sorrows of this world. Since you have long been ill, do not concern yourself with whether it heals or not; just have one thought, one mind — whether you live, let it be; whether you die, let it be.']

You should now set aside all those superfluous matters, concentrate your energy on holding the single phrase 'Amitabha Buddha,' never casting it aside for a single thought-moment; then Amitabha Buddha will be your good companion. When the great limit (the time of death) arrives, he will appear in person to guide your consciousness, and you will be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — how is this not better than entering the mountain to await death? Moreover, birth, aging, sickness, and death are the unavoidable sorrows of this world. Though you have long been ill, do not concern yourself with whether it heals or not; just be single-mindedly devoted to the one Buddha-name — whether you live, let it be; whether you die, let it be.'
Rather than passively entering the mountain to await death, it is better to actively recite the Buddha and seek rebirth — this is the choice of wisdom!
[Jingshan] Located about
kilometers northwest of Hangzhou, it is one of the five mountains of the world and enjoys great renown in Buddhism. [Putong stupa]
A stupa that gathers in one place the bones of deceased monks, and so is called the Putong (universal) stupa.

blocks.text: Submitting to a Teacher and Receiving the Precepts

inline.s: [The monk Bu'er was about to submit to a teacher and receive the precepts. The Bodhisattva said: 'What a pity! What a pity! With such an imposing appearance and such a fine bearing, you do not know how to reflect on yourself. Examining what you do, you are no different from an ordinary person. I see your body here, yet your spirit already wanders in hell! You must urgently apply yourself to austere self-cultivation and reflection, cut off evil and follow good, seek above the Buddha-fruit and guide below the multitudes of beings. Do not remain muddled and dim, squandering this limited time and bringing upon yourself the burden of ten thousand kalpas.']

The monk Bu'er was about to submit to a teacher and receive the precepts. The Bodhisattva said to him: 'What a pity! What a pity! With such an imposing appearance and such fine bearing, you yet do not know how to reflect on yourself. Examining your actions, you are no different from an ordinary person. I see your body here, yet you have already wandered in spirit to hell! You must urgently apply yourself to austere self-cultivation and reflection, cut off evil and follow good, seek above the Buddha-fruit and guide below the multitudes of beings. Do not remain muddled and dim, losing this limited time and bringing upon yourself the calamity of ten thousand kalpas.'
[As for
(as to)

the matter of receiving the precepts — if you do not receive them, then fine; but once you receive them, you must not transgress them in the slightest. You must guard them purely, like a white jade or a bright pearl, without the least flaw — only then does the precept-character attain fulfillment. For
(this is because)

the precepts are the fundamental entrance to the path for the Buddhas of the three times; do not treat them as child's play! Moreover, if you dwell in stillness or travel in search of masters, you should the more draw near good friends and distance yourself from the mediocre and inferior. Drawing near the good, the path is easy to accomplish; drawing near the evil, the precept-conduct is easy to lose. These two sayings are the essentials of a lifetime of studying the Way — be careful! Remember them!']

As for the matter of receiving the precepts — if you do not receive them, then it is fine; but once you have received them, you must not transgress them in the slightest. You must guard them purely, like a white jade or a bright pearl, without the least flaw, and only then can the precept-character be fulfilled. For the precepts are the fundamental entrance to the path for the Buddhas of the three times, and are no child's play! If you dwell in stillness in one place, or travel in search of masters, you should the more draw near good friends and distance yourself from those vulgar and inferior. Drawing near the good, the path is easy to accomplish; drawing near the evil, the precept-conduct is easy to lose. These two sayings (drawing near the good, the path is easy to accomplish; drawing near the evil, the precept-conduct is easy to lose) are the essential formulas of a lifetime of studying the Way — you must earnestly put them into practice and keep them in mind!'
For a cultivator, distancing himself from evil and drawing near the good is of utmost importance.
[Self-cultivation] To temper and develop one's moral character. [Flaw (
xiá diàn
A spot or crack in jade, a metaphor for a shortcoming or fault.
[The brothers Ma Yongxi, in a former life,
(a previous life)

were hunters. One day they entered the mountain and together killed a deer, and so were to receive the retribution of a short life. They also once saw the Buddha image in a stupa fall to the ground; they set it up on its seat, bowed, and left. Because of this wholesome cause, they again obtained a human body. The Bodhisattva first gave Yongxi instruction. Yongxi was afraid and sought the way
(longevity)
of a long life.']

The brothers Ma Yongxi, in a former life, were hunters. One day they entered the mountain and together killed a deer, and were to receive the retribution of a short life. They also once saw a Buddha image in a stupa lying on the ground; they set it up on its seat, bowed, and left. Because of this wholesome cause, they again obtained a human body. The Bodhisattva first gave Yongxi instruction. When Yongxi heard it, he was greatly frightened and sought from the Bodhisattva the way of longevity.

[The Bodhisattva said: 'In the past, at the Miaojue Temple in the north, there was a young novice, sixteen years old. There was a physiognomist who could tell of a person's life and death without the slightest error. He said to the novice: "In the last month of autumn of your eighteenth year
(the last month of autumn, the ninth month of the lunar calendar)
, you will die." The novice was greatly afraid. At night he prayed to the Buddha, wishing that from the canon
(the great Buddhist canon)

a sutra might be bestowed upon him, which he would hold for life, to pray for longevity. When he had spoken, he wept beyond endurance, bowed again, and rose. From the great canon he picked up at random the Prajna Sutra of the Diamond
(that is, the Diamond Sutra, whose full title is the Diamond Prajna-paramita Sutra)

. He then copied it and held it, without relaxation day or night. He also kept the precepts with strict purity and came to comprehend the profound principle. Before he was forty, his way of truth spread and flowed, and the four assemblies revered and looked up to him. Later he lived to eighty and passed away sitting upright. This was the Chan Master Weixing of Luoyang. It was a matter of the sixth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang, and I saw it myself.']

The Bodhisattva said: 'In the past, at the Miaojue Temple in the north, there was a young novice, sixteen years old. There was a physiognomist who could tell of a person's life and death without the slightest error. He said to the novice: "In the ninth month of your eighteenth year, you will die." The novice was greatly afraid. At night he prayed to the Buddha, wishing that from the great canon a single sutra might be bestowed upon him, which he would hold for life, to pray for longevity. When he had spoken, he wept beyond endurance, bowed again, and rose. From the great canon he picked up at random the Diamond Sutra. He then copied it and held it, without relaxation day or night, and also kept the precepts with strict purity, coming to comprehend the profound principle. Before he was forty, his way of truth spread and flowed, and the four assemblies revered and looked up to him. Later he lived to eighty and passed away sitting upright at ease. This was the Chan Master Weixing of Luoyang. It was a matter of the sixth year of the Kaiyuan era of Tang Emperor Xuanzong (
), and I saw it with my own eyes.'
[The four assemblies] Bhikshus, bhikshunis, upasakas, and upasikas.
[Bhikshu, bhikshuni]

Those who have left home and received the full precepts. The man is called a bhikshu, the woman a bhikshuni. [Upasaka] Translated into Chinese as the 'pure faithful man'; that is, a male lay disciple who in the world draws near and serves the Three Jewels and upholds the five precepts. [Upasika] Translated into Chinese as the 'pure woman'; that is, a female lay disciple who draws near and serves the Three Jewels and upholds the five precepts.

['Since you now fear a short life and seek a long life, you should, in accordance with this novice, obtain a good copy of the Diamond Sutra, set your mind on copying it, diligently recite it, and further seek to understand its purport — this is inner merit. From today onward, you must not again kill living beings; you should love them as your own body, and also accumulate much hidden virtue — this is outer merit. When both inner and outer are cultivated, the merit is very great; you can naturally unite with Heaven, and the principle of the non-duality of untimely death and long life is established — why worry that your years will not be long? Yet you must be careful to the end as at the beginning; like that novice, without remiss even at eighty, only then does one conform to the Way. Do not in any case have a head without a tail, or practice for ten days and half a month, one or two years, and then drop it. If you indeed reverently follow for your whole life
(without the slightest interruption)
, and your request is not fulfilled, then all the Buddhas and I will both have fallen into false speech.']

Since you now fear a short life and seek a long life, you should, in accordance with this novice, obtain a good copy of the Diamond Sutra (a copy whose text is clear and correct), set your mind on copying it (copying sutras was an important means of spreading the Dharma at that time), diligently practice and recite it, and further seek to understand its meaning — this is inner merit. From today onward, you must not kill any living being again, but should love life as your own body, and also accumulate much hidden virtue — this is outer merit. When both inner and outer are cultivated, the merit is very great; you can naturally unite with Heaven, and the principle of the non-duality of short life and long life is established — why worry that your life-span will not be long? Yet you must, from beginning to end, carefully practice both inner and outer, like that novice who was never remiss even at eighty; only then do you conform to the Way of Heaven. Do not in any case have a beginning without an end, or practice ten days and half a month, one year or two, and then throw it away. If indeed you reverently follow it for your whole bodily life, without interruption, and yet your request is not fulfilled, then all the Buddhas and I will both have fallen into false speech.'”

[Hidden virtue] Good (beneficial) deeds done for others in secret. [The non-duality of short life and long life] Whether one's life-span is short or long, it never changes. This saying comes from the Mencius

Jin Xin (I). The original text reads: 'Mencius said: One who exhausts his mind knows his nature. Knowing his nature, he knows Heaven. To preserve his mind and nourish his nature is how he serves Heaven. Whether one dies young or lives long, one never changes; cultivating oneself and awaiting (
sì

waiting for) it, this is how one establishes his destiny.' (The meaning of this passage: to exhaust one's loving-kindness of mind is to awaken to one's own original nature. Having awakened to one's own original nature, one knows Heaven. One should preserve one's benevolent mind and nourish one's own nature, and in this way serve Heaven. Whether one's life is short or long, it never changes; one merely cultivates oneself and nurtures one's nature to await Heaven's decree — this is how one shapes one's own destiny!) [Exhausting the body] To exhaust one's bodily life; to exhaust this life's form and life-span.

blocks.text: Holding the Resolve Over the Long Term

inline.s: [The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Dingzhuan
zhuān
the same as 'zhuan' — single-minded)

saying: 'It is most rare and difficult for you father and son to practice my teachings. But you must hold your resolve over the long term, and must not give rise to thoughts seeking a spiritual response. The two words "cultivation" should be practiced like the daily affairs of putting on clothes and eating rice — only then is it right.']
The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Dingzhuan (
zhuān

the same as 'zhuan' — single-minded): 'It is most rare and difficult for you father and son to practice my teachings. But you must arouse a long-term resolve, and must not give rise to thoughts seeking a spiritual response. The two words "cultivation" should be practiced until they are as indispensable as putting on clothes and eating rice in daily life.'
[Holding the resolve over the long term] The resolve to practice my teaching, enduring without change. [The long-term resolve] A heart that endures without change.

[The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dinghong's mother, saying: 'In the past you had a thought of seeking the Way, but you did not encounter a person of right understanding — this is deeply to be pitied. Now I shall give you clear instruction. In the past, when you were a bhikshu, you vigorously exerted yourself in practice, without relaxation day or night. Because your mind was fierce, in calm stillness a view suddenly arose: "Why can I not quickly attain Buddhahood?" Another day, hearing the words "The Buddhas are without marks; this very mind is the Buddha," you increased your wrong thought, saying: "Since all dharmas are empty and still, and my mind is the Buddha, what need is there to practice?" But you do not know that this is the ultimate emptiness-principle, and not something easily spoken of by one newly entering the Dharma-realm.']

The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dinghong's mother, saying: 'In the past you had a thought of seeking the Way, but you did not meet a true good friend — this is deeply to be pitied. Now I shall give you clear instruction. In the past, when you were a bhikshu, you vigorously exerted yourself in practice, without resting day or night. Because your mind's actions were fierce, in calm stillness a view suddenly arose: "Why can I not quickly attain Buddhahood?" Another day, hearing the words "The Buddhas are without marks; this very mind is the Buddha," you further increased your wrong thought, saying to yourself: "Since all dharmas are empty and still, and my mind is the Buddha, what need is there to practice?" But you do not know that this is the ultimate emptiness-principle, whose subtle meaning is not something a beginner can easily fathom.'
